name: Otto von Bismarck
summary: United Germany in three wars and then spent twenty years insuring it against the coalition those wars invited: the League of the Three Emperors, the alliance with Austria-Hungary, and the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 that kept a line open to St Petersburg. Wilhelm II dismissed him in March 1890 and let the treaty lapse; France and Russia allied in 1894. The two-front problem the Schlieffen Plan was written to answer is the shape Europe took after he left it.

name: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder

roles.title: Chief of the Prussian (from 1871 the Great) General Staff

summary: Chief of the General Staff for thirty years and the victor of 1864, 1866 and 1870 — the man who made the Prussian staff, the railway timetable and the mobilization plan into instruments of war. Two inheritances run from him into 1914: the two-front problem, which he answered with a defensive war in the west and limited offensives in the east rather than a knock-out blow, and the warning that no plan of operations survives the first encounter with the enemy's main body — the sentence the campaign that followed is measured against. Uncle of the younger Moltke who directed it.

name: Alfred von Schlieffen

roles.title: Chief of the German General Staff

summary: Chief of the German General Staff 1891–1906. His December 1905 memorandum — a massive right-wing sweep through Belgium and northern France to envelop the French armies — is the document the 1914 campaign is measured against, and whether it was ever an operational plan is itself a historiographical debate.

name: Helmuth von Moltke the Younger

roles.title: Chief of the German General Staff

summary: Schlieffen's successor, nephew of the victor of 1870. He modified the deployment — strengthening the left wing in Lorraine and, once war began, detaching corps to East Prussia and Antwerp — and directed the 1914 campaign from Koblenz and then Luxembourg. Relieved after the Marne.

name: Alexander von Kluck
summary: Commander of the German 1st Army on the outer edge of the right wing — the army that marched furthest and fastest, fought Mons and Le Cateau, wheeled inside Paris at the end of August and was struck on the Ourcq by Maunoury's 6th Army in September.

name: Karl von Bülow
summary: Commander of the German 2nd Army, for a time also directing the 1st and 3rd. Fought the Sambre and Guise; his decision to pull back from the Marne on 9 September, after Hentsch's visit, ended the campaign's offensive phase.

name: Max von Hausen
summary: Saxon commander of the German 3rd Army, the hinge between the right wing and the centre; forced the Meuse at Dinant and fought Foch's 9th Army in the marshes of Saint-Gond at the Marne before falling ill and being relieved.

name: Crown Prince Rupprecht of Bavaria
summary: Commander of the German 6th Army in Lorraine — the left wing that absorbed the French Plan XVII offensive at Morhange–Sarrebourg and then counterattacked toward the Trouée de Charmes and Nancy.

name: Richard Hentsch

roles.title: Head of intelligence, OHL; Moltke's emissary to the armies

summary: Lieutenant-colonel on the General Staff whom Moltke sent by car to the right-wing armies on 8–9 September 1914. His authority and the retreat order he sanctioned at 1st and 2nd Army headquarters are among the most argued-over moments of the campaign.

name: Erich Ludendorff

roles.title: Deputy chief of staff, German 2nd Army (Liège)
Chief of staff, German 8th Army (East Prussia)

summary: Staff officer who took Liège's citadel by bluff on 7 August 1914, then was sent east with Hindenburg to command at Tannenberg — the detour that links the western campaign to the eastern.

name: Erich von Falkenhayn

roles.title: Chief of the German General Staff

summary: Prussian Minister of War from 1913 and Chief of the General Staff from 14 September 1914 (in Moltke's place; officially from 3 November) to August 1916. He ran the Race to the Sea and the First Battle of Ypres in the autumn of 1914, then the war of attrition that culminated at Verdun in 1916; he was dismissed after Romania entered the war and commanded in Romania and Palestine.

name: Joseph Joffre
summary: Commander-in-Chief of the French armies 1914–1916: author of Plan XVII's frontier offensive, and of the retreat, the redeployment west by rail and the 6 September counterstroke that won the Marne.

name: Édouard de Castelnau
summary: Commander of the French 2nd Army in Lorraine: beaten at Morhange on 20 August, then held the Grand Couronné de Nancy through early September — the hinge that kept the German left from closing the other jaw.

name: Charles Lanrezac
summary: Commander of the French 5th Army on the Allied left. He read the German wheel through Belgium earlier than GQG, fought Charleroi and the counterattack at Guise on 29 August, and was replaced by Franchet d'Espèrey on 3 September.

name: Louis Franchet d'Espèrey
summary: Took over the French 5th Army on 3 September 1914 and drove it back north into the gap between Kluck and Bülow during the Marne; 'Desperate Frankie' to the British.

name: Michel-Joseph Maunoury
summary: Recalled from retirement to command the new French 6th Army, formed at the end of August from troops railed west. Its attack on Kluck's flank along the Ourcq on 5 September opened the Battle of the Marne.

name: Joseph Gallieni
summary: Military Governor of Paris from late August 1914. Saw the opening offered by Kluck's wheel, pushed Joffre to attack, and sent Maunoury's reinforcements forward — some of them in the requisitioned taxis that became the battle's legend.

name: Ferdinand Foch
summary: Commanded XX Corps in Lorraine, then the improvised 9th Army that held the marshes of Saint-Gond at the Marne. Later Allied generalissimo in 1918 — one person who spans the whole war.

name: Sir John French
summary: Commander of the British Expeditionary Force in 1914: Mons, Le Cateau, the retreat almost to the Seine, and — after Kitchener's intervention — the advance into the gap at the Marne.

name: Winston Churchill
summary: First Lord of the Admiralty in 1914; sent the Royal Naval Division to Antwerp in October and went there himself. Appears again at Gallipoli and, in 1940, as the figure the whole multi-era arc bends toward.

name: Albert I, King of the Belgians
summary: King and commander-in-chief who refused the German ultimatum, fought for the Gette line, withdrew the field army into Antwerp and held the Yser in October — keeping a corner of Belgium unoccupied for four years.

name: Gérard Leman

roles.title: Governor of the fortified position of Liège

summary: Commander of the Liège fortress ring. Held the forts against the German coup de main and the siege until the 42 cm howitzers broke them; carried unconscious from the ruins of Fort Loncin on 15 August.

name: Albrecht, Duke of Württemberg
summary: Heir to the throne of Württemberg and a career soldier, he commanded the German 4th Army through the Ardennes battles, the Marne and First Ypres, and from 1917 Army Group Albrecht on the southern end of the Western Front.

name: Wilhelm, German Crown Prince
summary: The Kaiser's eldest son commanded the 5th Army in 1914 — the Ardennes, Longwy and the Verdun sector — and in 1916 the army that attacked Verdun; from November 1916 he led Army Group Crown Prince. His chief of staff, Schmidt von Knobelsdorf, did much of the work.

name: Josias von Heeringen
summary: Prussian War Minister until 1913, then commander of the 7th Army in Alsace in 1914: Mulhouse, the Vosges and the Aisne after the army was moved north in September.

name: Auguste Dubail
summary: Commanded the French 1st Army on the right of Plan XVII — the advance into Alsace and Lorraine towards Sarrebourg, the retreat after Morhange, and the defence of the Vosges and the Trouée de Charmes; later commander of the Eastern Army Group.

name: Pierre Ruffey
summary: Commanded the French 3rd Army in the Ardennes offensive of 21–23 August around Longwy and Virton; relieved by Joffre on 30 August and replaced by Sarrail.

name: Fernand de Langle de Cary
summary: Commanded the French 4th Army into the Ardennes on 21–23 August (Neufchâteau, Rossignol), in the retreat over the Meuse and at the Marne around Vitry-le-François; later the Central Army Group and the early defence of Verdun.

name: Maurice Sarrail
summary: Took over the French 3rd Army from Ruffey on 30 August and held the line from Verdun to Revigny at the Marne, keeping the fortress as the hinge of the French right; the politically connected 'republican general' later commanded at Salonika.

name: Paul Pau
summary: A one-armed veteran of 1870 recalled from retirement to command the Army of Alsace, which retook Mulhouse on 19 August and was dissolved a week later when Joffre pulled its troops west for the new 6th Army.

name: Sir Douglas Haig
summary: Commanded I Corps of the BEF in 1914 — in reserve at Mons, the retreat from Landrecies to the Marne, the advance to the Aisne, and the defence of Ypres in October–November; commanded the First Army from December 1914 and the BEF from December 1915.

name: Sir Horace Smith-Dorrien
summary: Given II Corps on 21 August after Grierson died on the train to the front, he fought Mons on 23 August and, against Sir John French's wishes, stood and fought at Le Cateau on 26 August; commanded the Second Army from December 1914 until French removed him in May 1915.

name: Hans von Beseler
summary: Engineer general recalled from retirement to command the III Reserve Corps; turned off the wheel on 20 August to mask Antwerp, besieged and took the fortress in October 1914, and later governed occupied Poland.

name: Hans von Zwehl
summary: Commander of the VII Reserve Corps: besieged Maubeuge from 25 August to 7 September 1914, then force-marched the corps to the Chemin des Dames in time to close the gap between the 1st and 2nd Armies on 13 September — a day after the Marne was lost.

name: Joseph Anthelme Fournier

roles.title: Governor of the fortified position of Maubeuge

summary: Governor of Maubeuge; held the fortress against the VII Reserve Corps and the siege guns from 25 August to 7 September, longer than Liège or Namur, was court-martialled for the surrender like the other governors who had capitulated — and acquitted in May 1920.

name: Louis de Maud'huy

roles.title: Commanding, French Tenth Army (initially the Détachement d'armée de Maud'huy)

summary: French corps commander given the improvised army that Joffre pushed north to Arras at the beginning of October 1914 — the third of the successive attempts to find and turn the German northern flank. He held Arras when the attempt failed, and the town stayed in French hands for the rest of the war.

name: Victor d'Urbal

roles.title: Commanding, the French detachment in Belgium (Détachement d'armée de Belgique), which became the Eighth Army

summary: French cavalry general who commanded the French forces sent into Flanders in October 1914 — the divisions and territorials that fought beside the Belgians on the Yser and the British at Ypres. His command was regularised as the Eighth Army in November.

name: Pierre Ronarc'h
summary: French rear-admiral who took a brigade of naval reservists and Breton fishermen — the fusiliers marins — to Flanders in October 1914 and held Dixmude on the Yser for three weeks against far heavier forces, at the cost of most of the brigade.

name: Karel Cogge
summary: Belgian water bailiff of the Veurne polders, who knew which of the locks at Nieuwpoort would let the sea into the plain of the Yser and how far it would spread. In October 1914 he took that knowledge to the Belgian army; the inundation he helped open stopped the German advance at the last twenty kilometres of unoccupied Belgium.

name: Hendrik Geeraert
summary: Nieuwpoort bargeman who could work the sluice gates of the Ganzepoot lock complex in the dark and under fire, and did so on the nights of the last week of October 1914. Belgium later put his face on its banknotes.

name: Sophie Chotek
summary: A Bohemian countess whose marriage to the heir in 1900 was permitted only as morganatic: she could not share his rank, her children were barred from the throne, and at court she walked behind the youngest archduchess. On military inspections that protocol did not apply, which is part of why she was beside him in the car at Sarajevo on their fourteenth wedding anniversary. She was shot with him and died first.

name: Franz Ferdinand

roles.title: Heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne
Inspector General of the Austro-Hungarian armed forces

summary: Heir to the Habsburg throne and, on the evidence of his own papers, one of the more cautious voices in Vienna on war with Serbia - he had opposed the annexation crisis policy and doubted the army's readiness. He and his wife Sophie were shot at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip. His death removed the chief restraint on the war party at the moment it gave that party its occasion.

name: Gavrilo Princip

roles.title: Member of Mlada Bosna; assassin of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

summary: Bosnian Serb student, a member of the Young Bosnia circle, who shot the Archduke and Duchess at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 with a pistol supplied through Serbian military intelligence contacts. Too young for the death penalty, he was sentenced to twenty years and died of tuberculosis in the fortress of Theresienstadt in April 1918. How far his act was directed from Belgrade is one of the central disputes of the origins debate.

name: Leopold Berchtold
summary: Austro-Hungarian foreign minister through the July Crisis. He sought and obtained the German assurance of 5-6 July, presided over the drafting of the note to Serbia in terms meant to be refused, judged the Serbian reply of 25 July unsatisfactory, and pressed the declaration of war of 28 July - by his own account partly to foreclose the mediation proposals then circulating.

name: Nicholas II
summary: The last Russian emperor. On 29 July 1914 he ordered general mobilization, cancelled it within hours after a telegram from the Kaiser, and on 30 July let his ministers and the General Staff persuade him to order it again - the decision that, given the German deployment plan, made a European war all but certain. Overthrown in March 1917; murdered with his family at Ekaterinburg in July 1918.

name: Léon Raffenel
summary: Commanded the 3rd Colonial Infantry Division of the French 4th Army and was killed with most of his division at Rossignol on 22 August 1914, eight days after his fifty-eighth birthday — one of the first French general officers to die in the war.

name: Maurice Balfourier
summary: Took the French XX Corps — the Nancy corps, and the army's best — from Foch on 29 August 1914 and held the Grand Couronné with it through the September attacks; later commanded it at Verdun and on the Somme.

name: Wilhelm II

roles.title: German Emperor and King of Prussia

summary: German Emperor and nominal supreme warlord. In practice OHL made the operational decisions in 1914; the Kaiser travelled between headquarters, and came to Rupprecht's 6th Army in September expecting to ride into Nancy.

name: Victor Michel

roles.title: Vice-President of the Conseil superieur de la guerre (commander-in-chief designate)

summary: The French commander-in-chief designate who, in February 1911, proposed meeting a German attack through Belgium: a deployment reaching north to Lille and Mezieres, with reserve regiments paired to active ones to man the extra front. The Conseil superieur de la guerre rejected the plan as defensive and unaffordable in manpower, and he was moved to the Paris governorship within months; his successors built Plan XVII on the opposite assumption. He was relieved of Paris on 26 August 1914 and replaced by Gallieni.

name: Paul von Hindenburg
summary: Recalled from retirement on 22 August 1914 to command the Eighth Army in East Prussia, with Ludendorff as his chief of staff. Tannenberg made him the most famous soldier in Germany and, in time, the man who ran the war and then the republic that followed it.

name: Maximilian von Prittwitz
summary: Commanded the single army left to hold East Prussia. After Gumbinnen on 20 August he telephoned Moltke proposing to fall back behind the Vistula and abandon the province; he was relieved within two days, and the alarm he raised was still travelling when Moltke took two corps off the right wing to send east.

name: Max Hoffmann

roles.title: First General Staff Officer, German Eighth Army

summary: The staff officer who had the Eighth Army's plan of concentration against Samsonov ready before Hindenburg and Ludendorff arrived, and who spent the rest of his life saying so. Who deserves Tannenberg - Hoffmann, Ludendorff or the reputation Hindenburg took from it - is one of the war's longest-running arguments.

name: Alexander Samsonov
summary: Led the Second Army north-west into East Prussia, out of supply and out of touch with Rennenkampf on his right. When the encirclement closed he walked into the forest near Willenberg in the early hours of 30 August and shot himself.

sources.note: dates; the article gives Old Style dates alongside

name: Louis de Grandmaison

roles.title: Head of the Troisieme Bureau (operations), French General Staff

summary: Staff officer whose lectures of February 1911 gave the French doctrine of the offensive its slogan and its reputation. He argued that in an encounter battle the side that attacks first with everything imposes its will, and that caution costs more lives than audacity - the offensive a outrance written into the 1913 regulations and into the way French corps fought in August 1914. He was killed commanding a brigade in February 1915. Whether his lectures made the doctrine or merely named it is argued.

name: Paul von Rennenkampf
summary: Commanded the First Army, which entered East Prussia from the east and checked the Germans at Gumbinnen on 20 August - the victory that emptied the province of German nerve and then, when he did not pursue, left Samsonov to be destroyed alone.

name: Sir Henry Rawlinson
summary: British general sent to Belgium in October 1914 with an improvised corps - the 7th Division and the 3rd Cavalry Division - to relieve Antwerp, arriving too late for the city and occupying Ypres instead. His corps headquarters was withdrawn on 27 October and his divisions passed to Haig. He commanded the Fourth Army on the Somme in 1916 and in the advance of 1918.

sources.note: the IV Corps in Flanders, October 1914

name: Charles FitzClarence
summary: Irish-born brigadier-general, holder of the Victoria Cross from Mafeking, commanding the 1st (Guards) Brigade at Ypres. On the afternoon of 31 October 1914, with the line broken at Gheluvelt and two divisional staffs shelled out of their headquarters, he found the one battalion still in reserve and sent it to retake the village. He was killed leading a night counter-attack near Polygon Wood on 11/12 November.

sources.note: the order to the 2nd Worcesters on 31 October, and his death on the night of 11/12 November

name: Max von Fabeck
summary: German general given command, on 27 October 1914, of the force assembled between the Fourth and Sixth Armies for one more attempt on the Menin road - six divisions and the heaviest weight of artillery yet put behind an attack on that front. Its attack of 29-31 October broke the British line at Gheluvelt and could not get through the hole it made.

sources.note: the composition and the attack of Armeegruppe Fabeck, 29-31 October 1914

name: Chester W. Nimitz

roles.title: Commander in Chief, United States Pacific Fleet and Pacific Ocean Areas

summary: Took the Pacific Fleet ten days after its battle line was sunk at its moorings and fought the war the carriers and the submarines made possible rather than the one the pre-war plans described. Backed Rochefort's cryptanalysts against Washington's own estimate and put three carriers north-east of Midway on the strength of it; then ran the Central Pacific drive island by island towards bomber range of Japan, alternating Halsey's and Spruance's staffs over the same ships so that the fleet never had to stop to think. Signed the Japanese surrender for the United States aboard *Missouri* on 2 September 1945.

name: Ernest J. King

roles.title: Commander in Chief, United States Fleet

summary: Held both American naval commands at once — operational as Commander in Chief, United States Fleet and administrative as Chief of Naval Operations — and used them to stop the Pacific being adjourned. Germany-first was Allied policy and King never overturned it; what he did was keep enough shipping, escorts and Marines flowing west that the Guadalcanal landing of August 1942 could happen at all, eight months into a war the coalition had agreed to fight elsewhere first. Cordially disliked by almost everyone he worked with, which he treated as evidence he was doing the job.

name: William F. Halsey Jr.

roles.title: Commander, South Pacific Area and South Pacific Force

summary: The carrier admiral the American public knew by name, and the one the Navy sent where morale was the problem: the early raids on the Marshalls and the Doolittle launch in 1942, then the South Pacific command in October of that year, when Guadalcanal was being lost by degrees and was not lost after he arrived. Missed Midway in hospital with dermatitis and gave Spruance his carriers. At Leyte Gulf on 24–25 October 1944 he took the whole of Third Fleet north after Ozawa's aircraft-less carriers and left San Bernardino Strait unwatched; whether that was the decoy working as designed or a commander's error is the most argued single decision of the Pacific war.

name: Raymond A. Spruance

roles.title: Chief of Staff to Commander in Chief, Pacific Fleet

summary: A cruiser admiral with no aviation background who was handed Halsey's carriers three days before Midway and won the battle with them, launching at extreme range on an incomplete contact and then declining to chase Yamamoto's battleships into the night. The same refusal to be drawn made him the most criticised American admiral of June 1944, when he held Task Force 58 tied to the Saipan beachhead through the Philippine Sea instead of steaming west after Ozawa — the mirror image of the choice Halsey made four months later, and the reason the two decisions are always argued together.

name: Frank Jack Fletcher
summary: Commanded the American carriers in the first three carrier battles ever fought — Coral Sea, Midway and the Eastern Solomons — and lost *Lexington*, *Yorktown* and the argument about his own reputation. On 9 August 1942 he took his carriers away from the Guadalcanal beachhead citing fuel and fighter losses, leaving the transports uncovered on the night Savo Island was fought; Morison's verdict on that withdrawal hardened into the standard account and has been steadily revised since the 1990s, when historians began reading his fuel states rather than his critics. The reappraisal is one of the clearest cases in the theatre of an official history setting a man's record for fifty years.

name: Marc A. Mitscher

roles.title: Commander, Fast Carrier Task Force (Task Force 58 / 38)

summary: Captained *Hornet* for the Doolittle raid and then made Task Force 58 into the instrument that the Central Pacific drive ran on: fifteen carriers operating as one formation, capable of suppressing an island's air for a week and of destroying a fleet in a day. On the evening of 20 June 1944, with his aircraft returning from a strike at the limit of their fuel in the dark, he turned the task force's lights on — an order that gave away his position to submarines and got most of his pilots back, and which the men who flew that night never stopped repeating.

name: Douglas MacArthur

roles.title: Commanding General, United States Army Forces in the Far East
Supreme Commander, Allied Forces in the South West Pacific Area
Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Japan

summary: Lost the Philippines in 1942 having had nine hours' warning of Pearl Harbor and his air force caught on the ground at Clark Field regardless, was ordered out to Australia by Roosevelt, and spent the next two and a half years returning — up the New Guinea coast by a series of landings that went round Japanese garrisons rather than through them, and back to Leyte in October 1944. The Pacific had two commanders and no single one because neither the Navy nor MacArthur would serve under the other; the theatre was divided rather than the question settled, and the two axes of advance that resulted are the shape of the whole American campaign.

name: Alexander A. Vandegrift

roles.title: Commanding General, I Marine Amphibious Corps

summary: Landed the 1st Marine Division on Guadalcanal on 7 August 1942 with an incomplete plan, two-thirds of its supplies still in the transports when the transports left, and no assurance of naval cover; held the airfield perimeter for four months against attacks that came in nightly and in force, and was awarded the Medal of Honor for it. As Commandant after the war he fought the fight that decided the Marine Corps still existed, testifying against the 1946 unification proposals in a statement the Corps still quotes.

name: Holland M. Smith

roles.title: Commanding General, Fleet Marine Force, Pacific

summary: Wrote much of the American amphibious doctrine in the 1930s and then commanded the corps that executed it across the Central Pacific — Tarawa, the Marshalls, Saipan, Iwo Jima. Tarawa in November 1943 cost about a thousand Marines dead in seventy-six hours on an island of half a square mile, and the after-action reports from it changed naval gunfire, the length of the preparatory bombardment and the tracked landing vehicle. At Saipan in June 1944 he relieved an Army division commander, Major General Ralph Smith, in a row that reached the newspapers and left Army–Marine relations in the Pacific poisoned for the rest of the war.

name: Lewis B. Puller
summary: Battalion commander whose reputation was made on the night of 24–25 October 1942, when 1st Battalion, 7th Marines held about a thousand yards of the Guadalcanal perimeter against repeated regimental attacks by the Sendai Division and did not give way. Five Navy Crosses across three wars, the most awarded to any Marine, and the Corps' most quoted officer — which makes him a useful test of the difference between what a man did and what was later said about him.

name: Merritt A. Edson

roles.title: Chief of Staff, 2nd Marine Division (Tarawa, Saipan)

summary: Raised and commanded the 1st Marine Raider Battalion, and on the nights of 12–14 September 1942 held the ridge south of Henderson Field with about eight hundred Raiders and parachutists against Kawaguchi's brigade. The position was named after him afterwards; at the time he had chosen it himself, telling Vandegrift it was a good place for a rest camp because he did not want to say out loud that he expected the attack to come there. Medal of Honor for those two nights.

name: Evans F. Carlson

roles.title: Executive Officer, 4th Marine Regiment / operations officer, 4th Marine Division

summary: Spent 1937–38 marching with the Chinese Eighth Route Army, came home convinced that a small unit could be led by explanation rather than by orders, and built the 2nd Marine Raider Battalion on the idea — including the phrase he brought back with him, *gung ho*. Took the battalion ashore on Makin in August 1942 and then on the thirty-day Long Patrol behind the Japanese lines on Guadalcanal that November. The Chinese years made him suspect to his own service for the rest of his life, and the Raider battalions were disbanded in 1944.

name: Joseph J. Rochefort

roles.title: Officer in Charge, Combat Intelligence Unit (Station HYPO), 14th Naval District

summary: Ran Station HYPO in the basement at Pearl Harbor, the combat intelligence unit that was reading enough of the Japanese fleet code by May 1942 to say that the objective designated AF was Midway — and proved it by having Midway signal in clear that its distillation plant had failed and then reading the Japanese report that AF was short of water. Washington's own analysts had said the Aleutians or the south-west Pacific. Nimitz believed Rochefort, and the battle was fought where he said it would be. The Distinguished Service Medal Nimitz recommended was blocked in Washington; it was awarded in 1986, ten years after Rochefort's death.

name: John Basilone

roles.title: Gunnery Sergeant, 1st Battalion, 27th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: Machine-gun section leader in 1st Battalion, 7th Marines on Guadalcanal on the night of 24–25 October 1942, when his two sections were reduced to a handful of men and he kept the guns firing, repaired one under fire and carried ammunition up through the Japanese positions; Medal of Honor for it. Sent home to sell war bonds, he asked repeatedly to be returned to a rifle company, got his way, and was killed in the first hours on Iwo Jima on 19 February 1945 leading a machine-gun platoon off the beach. Navy Cross, posthumously — the only enlisted Marine of the war to hold both decorations.

name: Doris Miller

roles.title: Mess Attendant, later Cook Third Class, USS *West Virginia* (BB-48)

summary: A mess attendant on *West Virginia* — the rating the Navy reserved for Black sailors, who were not permitted to serve in a gunnery rate — who on the morning of 7 December 1941 carried wounded men clear, helped move his mortally wounded captain, and then fired a .50-calibre anti-aircraft gun he had never been trained on until the ammunition ran out. Nimitz pinned the Navy Cross on him aboard *Enterprise* on 27 May 1942, the first to a Black sailor. He was still a cook when *Liscome Bay* was torpedoed off Makin on 24 November 1943 and went down with her.

name: Frederick C. Branch

roles.title: Private, later Sergeant, 51st Defense Battalion, USMC
Second Lieutenant, United States Marine Corps Reserve

summary: One of the roughly twenty thousand Black Marines trained at Montford Point, the segregated camp outside Camp Lejeune where the Corps sent them after 1942 rather than to Parris Island. Served in the Pacific with the 51st Defense Battalion, and on 10 November 1945 — the Corps' birthday — was commissioned second lieutenant, the first African American officer in the history of the Marine Corps. Montford Point Marines carried ammunition and fought at Saipan, Peleliu and Iwo Jima in units the Corps had insisted would never see combat.

name: Chester Nez

roles.title: Private, later Corporal, code talker, United States Marine Corps

summary: One of the original twenty-nine Navajo recruited by the Marine Corps in May 1942 to build a code out of their own language — a vocabulary of several hundred terms improvised in a room at Camp Elliott, in which a submarine was an iron fish and a dive bomber a chicken hawk, layered over an alphabet of Navajo words. He carried it through Guadalcanal, Bougainville, Guam and Peleliu. The code was never broken. It stayed classified until 1968, so the men who made it came home to twenty-three years of not being able to say what they had done; Nez had been beaten at boarding school for speaking the language the Corps then asked him for.

name: Ann A. Bernatitus

roles.title: Lieutenant, Navy Nurse Corps, Philippines (Cañacao, Bataan, Corregidor)

summary: Navy nurse at Cañacao, then at Army Field Hospital No. 1 on Bataan through the retreat and the surrender fighting, then on Corregidor, operating in a tunnel under bombardment on a diet that had been cut to a third of a ration. Evacuated by the submarine *Spearfish* on 3 May 1942, days before the fortress fell; the eighty-odd Army and Navy nurses left behind spent the next three years interned at Santo Tomas and Los Baños. She was the first person awarded the Legion of Merit.

name: Ruby G. Bradley

roles.title: Lieutenant, Army Nurse Corps, Camp John Hay, Philippines
Interned civilian and prisoner, Camp Holmes and Santo Tomas Internment Camp

summary: Army nurse captured at Camp John Hay in northern Luzon three weeks into the war and interned for thirty-seven months, most of them at Santo Tomas in Manila, where she assisted at hundreds of operations and delivered babies in a camp that was starving by 1944 — the internees called the nurses who kept working the Angels of Bataan, though most of them, like her, had never been on Bataan. She smuggled food to children in the pockets of her uniform and weighed under six stone when the 1st Cavalry Division reached the camp in February 1945. Stayed in the Army, ran the nursing in Korea, and retired the most decorated woman in American military history.

name: George T. Sullivan
summary: The eldest of the five Sullivan brothers of Waterloo, Iowa, who enlisted together after a friend was lost at Pearl Harbor on the condition that they serve on the same ship, and were assigned to the light cruiser *Juneau*. She was torpedoed off Guadalcanal on 13 November 1942 and blew up; four brothers died at once and George, the last, survived several days in the water. Their mother was told by a letter that arrived with no notification of which sons. The Navy's later sole-survivor policy, and its reluctance ever again to berth brothers together, dates from them.

name: Joe Rosenthal
summary: Associated Press photographer who had been rejected by the Army for his eyesight and photographed the Pacific instead. On the morning of 23 February 1945 he climbed Suribachi behind the patrol carrying the second, larger flag, framed six men raising it in about a fifteenth of a second, and did not know what he had until the picture reached New York. Asked days later whether the photograph had been posed, he answered yes about a different picture — a group shot he had taken afterwards — and the confusion followed him for sixty years. He also photographed the first flag's raisers coming down, which is part of why the identifications took so long to settle.

name: Ernie Pyle
summary: The correspondent who wrote the war from the level of the private soldier — names, home towns, what the food was like, who had been killed — in a syndicated column that ran in hundreds of American papers and won the Pulitzer in 1944. He covered North Africa, Sicily, Italy and Normandy, came to the Pacific reluctantly in 1945 saying he was afraid he had used himself up, and was killed by a machine-gun burst on Ie Shima off Okinawa on 18 April 1945. The men of the 77th Division buried him there under a board that read: at this spot the 77th Infantry Division lost a buddy.

name: Eugene B. Sledge

roles.title: Private First Class, Company K, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, 1st Marine Division

summary: Dropped out of officer training to make sure he saw the war, and served as a 60 mm mortarman in K Company, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines through Peleliu and Okinawa — the two longest and least explicable battles the 1st Marine Division fought. He kept notes in the margins of a pocket Bible because keeping a diary was forbidden, and turned them thirty-five years later into *With the Old Breed*, the account historians reach for when they want to say what the ground was actually like. He became a biology professor and did not talk about it for decades.

name: Michael Strank

roles.title: Sergeant, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: Born in a village in what is now Slovakia and brought to the Pennsylvania coalfields at three; a Marine since 1939 and the sergeant who led the four-man detail up Suribachi on 23 February 1945 with the second flag. He is the figure at the back of Rosenthal's photograph, the only one of the six whose identification has never been questioned, and the only one who was a regular rather than a wartime enlistment. Killed by an American shell six days later, on 1 March, while sketching a plan for his squad in the sand. He had been made a United States citizen automatically by his father's naturalisation and was never told.

name: Harlon Block

roles.title: Corporal, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: A Texan who enlisted with his whole high-school football team, and the man at the base of the flagstaff in Rosenthal's photograph. The Marine Corps identified that figure as Sergeant Henry Hansen and said so for two years. Ira Hayes, who had been there, said it was Block, was told to be quiet, and in 1946 hitchhiked and walked the last miles to the Block farm in Weslaco to tell his mother she had been right; the Corps re-examined the picture and corrected the record in January 1947. Block had been killed on 1 March 1945, the same day as Strank, and did not know he was in the photograph at all.

name: Ira Hayes

roles.title: Private First Class, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: Akimel O'odham from the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona, a parachute-qualified Marine who fought at Bougainville and Iwo Jima and is the figure with his hands open at the left of Rosenthal's photograph. He insisted, against the Corps' own identification and at cost to himself, that the man at the base of the pole was Harlon Block and not Henry Hansen, and made the correction stick. Sent home on the bond tour, he asked to be returned to his unit; the tour and what followed it never let go, and he died of exposure and alcohol on the reservation in January 1955, aged thirty-two. He is the reason the record was corrected the first time and part of the reason it was looked at again seventy years later.

name: Franklin Sousley

roles.title: Private First Class, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: A Kentucky farm boy of nineteen, in the photograph between Hayes and Strank. He was killed by a sniper near Kitano Point on 21 March 1945, nine days before the island was declared secure; the telegram reached his mother at the general store in Hilltop and the neighbours heard her from the road. His identification in the picture was among those the Marine Corps re-examined in 2019, and it stood.

name: Harold H. Schultz

roles.title: Private First Class, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: A Detroit Marine wounded on Iwo Jima on 13 March 1945, discharged, and employed for thirty years by the Los Angeles post office. In June 2016 a Marine Corps board concluded from photogrammetric comparison of uniforms, weapons and equipment — work begun by two amateur researchers examining the frames around Rosenthal's — that Schultz, and not the Navy corpsman John Bradley, was the second figure from the left in the photograph. He appears to have known. Once, late in his life, he said at a dinner table that he had been one of the flag raisers, and when his stepdaughter asked, said only: I was.

name: Harold P. Keller

roles.title: Corporal, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: An Iowa farmer who had been a Marine Raider before the Raider battalions were broken up into the 5th Marine Division. In October 2019 a second Marine Corps board found that the figure previously identified as Rene Gagnon — the third man from the left, partly hidden — was Keller. He came home, went back to farming near Brooklyn, Iowa, and told his family almost nothing; his daughter learned he was in the photograph from the 2019 announcement, twenty-eight years after his death.

name: John H. Bradley

roles.title: Pharmacist's Mate Second Class, USN, attached to 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines

summary: A Navy pharmacist's mate attached to the 28th Marines, awarded the Navy Cross on Iwo Jima for treating wounded men in the open under fire, and identified for seventy-one years as one of the six in Rosenthal's photograph. He was on Suribachi that morning and helped with the **first** flag, which is what the 2016 board concluded he is seen doing in the other photographs of the day; the man in Rosenthal's frame was Harold Schultz. Bradley was sent on the bond tour, came home to Antigo, Wisconsin, ran a funeral home and refused interviews for the rest of his life. His son's book *Flags of Our Fathers* is the reason most people know the story, and the correction landed after both of them were dead.

name: Rene A. Gagnon

roles.title: Private First Class, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division

summary: A mill-town Marine from Manchester, New Hampshire, who carried the second flag up Suribachi in his pack and was one of the three survivors sent home to raise money on the strength of the photograph. He was identified as one of the raisers from 1945 until October 2019, when the Marine Corps concluded the figure was Harold Keller. Gagnon supplied several of the original identifications himself in Washington in April 1945, from memory, days after the event and under considerable pressure — which is how the misidentifications entered the record in the first place, and why the story is less about deceit than about what was being asked of nineteen-year-olds in a bond drive.

name: Yamamoto Isoroku

names.name: Isoroku Yamamoto
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

summary: Opposed the war he then planned. He had been a student at Harvard and a naval attaché in Washington, argued against the Tripartite Pact until his life was threatened by the ultranationalist right, and told the prime minister in 1940 that he could run wild for six months or a year but had no confidence in the second and third. He built the Pearl Harbor plan on that estimate — a single blow to buy the time — and pressed the Midway operation as the decisive battle that would end the war before American production made it unwinnable. Killed on 18 April 1943 when American fighters, flying on decrypted itinerary traffic, shot down his aircraft over Bougainville.

name: Nagumo Chūichi

names.name: Chuichi Nagumo
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Commander, Central Pacific Area Fleet, Saipan

summary: A torpedo and surface-warfare officer with no aviation background, given the First Air Fleet — the six-carrier striking force that was the most powerful naval formation in the world — because seniority said so. He commanded it from Pearl Harbor through the Indian Ocean to Midway, doubted every operation he was given, and at Midway on 4 June 1942 lost four carriers in a morning while trying to rearm his reserve aircraft between an unexpected land attack and a late American contact report. The picture of decks packed with fuelled aircraft comes from Fuchida and is not what the Japanese records show. He killed himself on Saipan on 6 July 1944.

name: Yamaguchi Tamon

names.name: Tamon Yamaguchi
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

summary: Commanded the Second Carrier Division — *Hiryū* and *Sōryū* — and was widely expected to command the Combined Fleet one day. At Midway, with the other three carriers burning, he launched what he had left in two small strikes that found *Yorktown* and put her out of the battle; *Hiryū* was then found and hit in turn. He refused to leave her, telling the crew to abandon ship and staying aboard as she was scuttled before dawn on 5 June 1942. The Imperial Navy lost four carriers at Midway and could replace them; it could not replace the aircrew or him.

name: Ozawa Jisaburō

names.name: Jisaburō Ozawa
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

summary: The Imperial Navy's most thoughtful carrier commander, and the one who inherited the arm after its aircrew had been used up. In the Philippine Sea in June 1944 he attacked at ranges his aircraft could reach and American aircraft could not, and lost about four hundred of them in a day to radar-directed fighters and proximity-fuzed anti-aircraft fire; the Americans called it the Marianas Turkey Shoot. Four months later at Leyte he took what was left of the carriers north with almost no aircraft aboard, as a decoy, and it worked: Halsey went after him and left San Bernardino Strait open. Ozawa's fleet existed by then to be sacrificed, and he knew it.

name: Kurita Takeo

names.name: Takeo Kurita
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Commander, Second Fleet (Centre Force at Leyte Gulf)

summary: Took the Centre Force — five battleships including *Yamato* and *Musashi* — through the Sibuyan Sea under air attack, lost *Musashi*, came through San Bernardino Strait in the dark, and at dawn on 25 October 1944 found himself off Samar with nothing between him and the Leyte landings but six escort carriers and their destroyers. He fought them for two and a half hours, took the destroyers' suicidal torpedo attacks for a fleet action, and turned north and away. Why he turned is the unanswered question of Leyte Gulf: exhaustion after three days of being bombed, a false report of a carrier force to the north, or a decision that the ships were worth more than the beachhead.

name: Saitō Yoshitsugu

names.name: Yoshitsugu Saitō
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Commanding General, 43rd Division; senior army commander, Saipan

summary: Commanded the 43rd Division and the army garrison on Saipan, where the Japanese defence changed the war's arithmetic: about thirty thousand defenders, almost none of whom surrendered, and a civilian population of some twenty thousand Japanese settlers who had been told what Americans did to prisoners. His last order told the garrison there was no longer any distinction between advancing and dying, and the banzai attack of 7 July 1944 was the largest of the war. He killed himself the same week. What followed on the cliffs at Marpi Point — civilians going over the edge in front of American loudspeakers begging them not to — is the reason Saipan is the hinge of the whole argument about how the war would have to be ended.

name: Kuribayashi Tadamichi

names.name: Tadamichi Kuribayashi
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Commanding General, 109th Division and Ogasawara Army District (Iwo Jima)

summary: Had spent two years in the United States in the 1920s and told his family that America was the last country Japan should fight. Given Iwo Jima in June 1944, he threw out the doctrine that had failed everywhere else — no defence at the waterline, no banzai charge — and spent eight months digging eleven miles of tunnels into the volcanic rock, so that the island itself was the fortification and the Americans would have to take it a bunker at a time. He forbade suicide attacks and told the garrison each man was to kill ten. The battle cost the Marine Corps more casualties than it inflicted, the only such battle of the Pacific war. His letters home, about the kitchen floor and his daughter's schooling, were published in Japan in 2005.

name: Ushijima Mitsuru

names.name: Mitsuru Ushijima
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

summary: Commanded the Thirty-Second Army on Okinawa and fought the same battle Kuribayashi had, on a larger island with a civilian population on it. He let the Americans land unopposed on 1 April 1945 and held the fortified lines across the southern third of the island — Kakazu, Shuri, the Yaeju-Dake — for eighty-two days, which was the point: every day bought was a day the invasion of the home islands was delayed. Around a quarter of Okinawa's civilians died in the ground fighting, and the campaign's cost on both sides is cited by both sides of the argument about the atomic bombs. He killed himself on 22 June 1945 as the line reached the southern cliffs.

name: Fuchida Mitsuo

names.name: Mitsuo Fuchida
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Commander, air group, First Air Fleet; strike leader at Pearl Harbor

summary: Led the air attack on Pearl Harbor and sent the signal *tora tora tora* to say surprise had been achieved. Appendicitis kept him out of the cockpit at Midway and he watched the four carriers burn from *Akagi*'s deck. After the war he became the principal English-language witness to the Japanese side of both battles — and one of the least reliable: the packed flight decks, the five fateful minutes, his own account of being about to launch when the dive bombers arrived, are all contradicted by the Japanese operational records, and *Shattered Sword* traced how completely his version had been absorbed into the Western literature. He became a Christian evangelist in 1950 and toured the United States preaching.

name: Sakamaki Kazuo

names.name: Kazuo Sakamaki
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Ensign, Special Attack Unit, Imperial Japanese Navy

summary: Ensign in command of one of the five midget submarines launched against Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. His gyrocompass failed, he grounded twice, could not fire either torpedo, and was washed ashore unconscious at Waimanalo the next morning — prisoner of war number one, the first man the United States captured in the Pacific war. He asked to be allowed to kill himself and was refused. Four years in American camps turned him from a man who had trained to die into one who argued against dying, and after the war he ran the Brazilian subsidiary of Toyota. He did not speak publicly about it until 1991, when he saw his own submarine in a museum.

name: Ōba Sakae

names.name: Sakae Ōba
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Captain, 18th Infantry Regiment, Imperial Japanese Army, Saipan

summary: A schoolteacher conscripted in 1934 and a captain by 1944, when he came ashore on Saipan as a survivor of a sunk transport. After the banzai attack of 7 July and the fall of the island he took to the interior of Mount Tapochau with about forty-six soldiers and some two hundred civilians, and stayed there. He kept them alive by raiding American supply dumps, evaded the sweeps sent after him, and finally marched his men down and surrendered in formation on 1 December 1945 — three months after the war ended, and only when a former superior officer was brought to Saipan to give him the order in person. The Americans called him the Fox of Saipan.

name: Yokoi Shōichi

names.name: Shoichi Yokoi
names.period: given-name-first order, as English-language catalogues index him

roles.title: Holdout in the interior of Guam

summary: A tailor from Aichi conscripted in 1941 and sent to Guam, where the garrison was destroyed in August 1944. He went into the jungle and stayed there for twenty-eight years, living for most of them alone in a cave he had dug beside a river, wearing cloth he wove from tree bark on a loom he made. Two fishermen found him in January 1972. He came home to a country he did not recognise and said the sentence that made him famous — that he was ashamed to have returned alive — and it is worth setting beside the men who went over the cliffs at Marpi Point, because it is the same instruction, obeyed by a conscript who had wanted none of it.

name: Vladimir Lenin

names.name: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov
names.period: the name he was born with

roles.title: Leader of the Bolshevik faction, Russian Social Democratic Labour Party
Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars

summary: A lawyer's son from Simbirsk who spent most of his adult life in exile arguing about organisation, and who arrived at the argument that a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries was the necessary instrument of a revolution rather than its expression. He was in Zurich when the Tsar fell and reached Petrograd only in April 1917, having crossed Germany in a sealed carriage the German government was glad to provide. From that April his position - no support for the Provisional Government, no continuation of the war, all power to the Soviets - was for six months a minority view even inside his own party, and by October it was the majority view in the capital. He headed the government that resulted until his health broke in 1922.

name: Leon Trotsky

names.name: Lev Davidovich Bronstein
names.period: the name he was born with

roles.title: Chairman of the St Petersburg Soviet

summary: A Ukrainian farmer's son who had chaired the St Petersburg Soviet in 1905 at twenty-six, spent the years between in exile writing about permanent revolution, and stood outside both wings of Russian social democracy until the summer of 1917, when he joined the Bolsheviks. Elected chairman of the Petrograd Soviet in September, he chaired the Military Revolutionary Committee that took the capital in October, negotiated at Brest-Litovsk, and built the Red Army. He lost the succession to Stalin, was expelled and deported, wrote the fullest participant's history of the revolution, and was murdered in Mexico in 1940.

name: Alexander Kerensky

roles.title: Deputy for Saratov, Fourth State Duma
Minister of War and the Navy

summary: A defence lawyer who had made his name in political trials, the only man to sit in both the Duma Committee and the Petrograd Soviet in the first days of the revolution, and the figure through whom the two halves of dual power were briefly joined. He rose in eight months from Minister of Justice to head of government and Supreme Commander, staked the government on a summer offensive that failed, quarrelled fatally with his own Supreme Commander in August, and left Petrograd by car on the morning of 25 October (O.S.) to find troops that did not come. He lived another fifty-three years, most of them in the United States, arguing his case.

name: Lavr Kornilov

roles.title: Supreme Commander of the Russian Army

summary: A Siberian Cossack officer, an explorer of Turkestan and a military attache in Peking before the war, who escaped from Austrian captivity in 1916 and came out of it a public figure. Appointed Supreme Commander in the summer of 1917 to restore discipline, he sent a cavalry corps towards Petrograd in late August in circumstances that have been argued about ever since, was declared a rebel by the head of the government who had wanted the troops, and was arrested. He escaped to the Don, helped found the Volunteer Army, and was killed by a shell at Ekaterinodar in April 1918.
